### PART 25: THE MECHANISM'S REACH — IN APPENDIX S
The comparative examination of the mechanism's reach — the tiered record, the phenomena examined, the dedicated evidence runs and the target programme — belongs to the optional scientific programme and is kept whole in Appendix S under its original numbers, so that every reference to Part 25 finds it there (Core L-489).

### PART 26: STRUCTURAL VOCABULARY (SELECTED ADDITIONS)
This Part catalogues terms the protocol uses but has not, until now, formally defined in one place. It is a selected set, not an exhaustive one; cultural and religious terms are not included here, since reducing concepts many people hold with real weight to a structural position risks reading as dismissive of that weight.
General rule for position names. Whenever a position name (Seed, Fixpoint, Observer, Navigator, Time, Reckoning, and so on) carries structural weight in a reading, the reading should say whether the weight comes from the position's index and orbit value (CDT-A, invariant under relabeling) or from the name itself (CDT-B, a design choice — see Core Part 1.6, tier note). Both are legitimate grounds for a reading; only the first survives if the name were changed.
Typed coordinates: a position (P8), its index (i(P8) = 8), its orbit value (v(P8) = 5) and its character (c(P8) = Generation) are four objects; offsets use indices, value arithmetic uses orbit values, and characters never enter arithmetic (Core Part 1.6).
Question and Answer: unqualified, the Question is the anchor position (always P1–P9) and the Answer its antipode (always P13–P21). Four other things share the words: the Striker's question (the verbatim domain), THE ANSWER (the output section), the 1/7 Aperture (the Striker's judgment), and, in philosophy, the general relation of asking and answering (Part 33.11).
Seed: P0, and the seed pair {2,5} from which the recurrence unfolds the 24-cycle. The 1/7 is not a seed in this sense; in the projection reading it is the origin from which the periphery is read (Core Part 0.14.4).
The Kernel: the 9 state pairs in (Z/9Z)² where both components are nilpotent {3,6,9} — the Fix and Wheel orbits together. Structurally unreachable by the canonical Voice C anchor (FP-KernelCrown, Core Specification Part 1.8).
The Quotient / The Cover / The Lift: the reduction map Z/9Z → Z/3Z induces a 9-to-1 cover of the full state space. The quotient is the resulting 8-state cycle. Each period-24 voice is a 3-to-1 lift of that quotient cycle; the three voices together form the full 9-to-1 lift.
The Trace: the countable boundary-drawing events a verbatim domain records — its words, letters, syllables. The protocol reads the trace; the Striker authors the meaning. "Trace" is also the protocol's own CDT-B shorthand name for a navigation (Preamble, Q13).
The Strike: the Striker's act of bringing a verbatim domain to the protocol — the entry point of every navigation, and the act the Striker is named for.
Doubt: the structural act of striking an alternative phrasing (M116, Core Specification Step 13). A reading that survives the strike is robust on this domain; one that does not is phrasing-sensitive.
Belief: the assumption of the postulate for the duration of a navigation (Rule 1). Procedural, not psychological — the Navigator does not believe the postulate in any ordinary sense; it operates as though it holds because the navigation requires that ground to run at all.
Error: a detected departure from the frozen specification, flagged with an NCF identifier and caught by the protocol's own verification instruments (M210, M268, M213, M214, M219, M224, M270). Structurally auditable by design.
Identity: a domain's anchor position. Two domains sharing an anchor share a structural identity within the frame, independent of what either domain is about.
Cause / Causality: two structurally distinct regimes within the 24-cycle. The Causal Zone (P0–P17) is where a position's structure follows from what precedes it. The Retrocausal Zone (P18–P23) is where the Möbius Twist is active and a position is shaped by what it becomes.
Death [EXPLORATORY — CDT-C]: the structural crossing from the Causal Zone into the Retrocausal Zone — a fold in the cycle's own structure, not, in this reading, an ending.
---

### PART 27: COMMUNITY VOCABULARY [EXPLORATORY — CDT-C]
These are informal, community-facing terms, offered for whoever comes to practice with Omega42 once it is public. They describe experiences a Striker has, not protocol mechanics. They are not operative: they do not constrain a Navigator's output, they do not enter SR-CAS, and they carry no weight in any formal instrument. They are not frozen: a community that forms around the protocol may refine, replace, or abandon any of them, the way any living vocabulary changes under actual use. They do not pre-empt or replace Part 10's operative abbreviations, which remain the only vocabulary a Navigator's output is bound by.
A term earns a place here only if it names a recurring unnamed experience. Synonyms for existing formal measurements do not qualify; neither do transient, idiosyncratic usages, nor judgments of the frame itself. "The reading felt hollow" would be a claim about the protocol, not a report of an experience, and does not belong here.
Landing — a synthesis that feels immediately and strikingly apt; the reading the Striker recognizes as connecting. This is the Striker's own recognition, not the Navigator's assessment of its output and not a formal score. Two people can strike the same domain, receive the same structural reading, and only one has a Landing. The word echoes IN-05's own "let us see where it lands."
Miss — a synthesis that was coherent but did not connect for the Striker. This is a Striker experience, distinct from two things it is sometimes confused with: a Fallback, which is the procedural outcome when no version of THE ANSWER passes all seven gates (Step 14.1) — and Sensitive, which is what M116 reports when an alternative phrasing shifts the anchor (a low CFR). A Miss is a reading that reached the Striker and did not land; the other two are not Striker experiences at all.
Recoil — a synthesis that lands, and the Striker recognizes it, and doesn't welcome it. The reading is apt; the aptness is unwelcome. This is a third outcome distinct from both Landing and Miss, and often the most memorable one in practice.
Twin — two unrelated domains landing on the same anchor. This is the community's way of noticing what M115 formally records as an "Identical" result (distance D=0); the measurement is M115's, the noticing and the word for it are the community's. Whether a given Twin feels surprising or unsurprising is left to the community to further distinguish, if it wants to.
Crossing — one domain's arm (Yang, Yin, 4D, or Antipode) lands on the anchor of a different domain the same Striker has navigated. This is not a Twin: a Twin is anchor meeting anchor; a Crossing is an arm meeting an anchor, a bridge between two separate navigations rather than a coincidence within one. Chains of Crossings across several navigations are left for a community to name, if it wants to, once it finds them.
Slippery — a domain whose reading shifts substantially when rephrased; the Striker tries a few phrasings and gets a few different anchors. The formal properties underneath this (L4, L7–L10) and the formal instruments that measure it (M116, M238) already exist; "Slippery" is the light word for what it feels like to run into that property firsthand, and carries no verdict about whether the domain or the phrasing is at fault.
Facing (alternate: Pairing) — deliberately striking a domain and its known Antipode together, to see the complementary structure play out on purpose. "Facing" is offered alongside "Pairing" as a second candidate rather than a single fixed choice, since which word a community adopts for a spontaneous practice is not something to decide in advance of anyone practicing it.

### PART 28: THREE SCENARIOS FOR OMEGA42'S FUTURE [EXPLORATORY — CDT-C]
Status note: this Part is CDT-C, but of a different kind than the readings elsewhere in this Companion. Parts like the Ten Philosophical Branches (Part 23) each extend a specific Fact or FP already established; this Part illustrates a spectrum of outcomes rather than extending a structural finding, and carries no evidentiary weight on its own. It should not be read as a prediction, and the central and higher-support outcomes are not the direction the other evidence points — the baseline outcome is as likely as either, by anything stated so far.
This Part states three points on a single spectrum of how far Omega42, in its use as an instrument of comparative research, could plausibly go [COMPARATIVE mode: one of its uses, never its purpose or the measure of a navigation, Core L-522, L-539 (1)] — not as a prediction, and not as outcomes the protocol's architecture guarantees any of, but as the range stated in advance. The Companion's own treatment of the corpus (the APE Commons and Part 24) and Part 25's examination of the mechanism's reach ground four coherent readings of the human-AI relation, synthesized here rather than established elsewhere in either document: Complementarity, in which the 1/7 Aperture remains distinctly the Striker's; Amplified Mirror, in which sovereignty is preserved on paper but eroded by an increasingly influential model of the human; Two-Frame System, in which the human becomes one of two poles rather than the sole locus of meaning; and Convergence, in which the frames merge as each is increasingly trained on the other. Part 28.1 states the baseline outcome, in which the project succeeds at its most specific aim. Part 28.2 states the central outcome, built on Complementarity, in which the project succeeds at what this Companion treats as its most natural reading. Part 28.3 states the higher-support outcome, in which the evidence goes further than either of the others has reason to expect. None of the three is the default outcome; each names what would have to be true, and what would have to be built, for that version of events to be the one that holds.

### 28.1 Scenario A — Baseline Outcome
CRC-60 either never gets built, or is built and the mining protocol finds nothing that survives its own null-model check: every pattern visible in the Omega42 corpus also appears in ordinary AI outputs on comparable content outside the protocol's constraint, meaning the constraint itself produced nothing distinctive. The reach record stays at the placement depth indefinitely, or the rules are revised under the stated conditions of Part 216.4 — SR-CAS scores that do not exceed chance, or Strikers who consistently find no useful guidance in what the structural reading produces. Cross-architecture convergence turns out to be no higher than what any two large language models would show on the same input regardless of Omega42's coordinate.
Under this outcome, the corpus's value is specific: a well-documented dataset of how a handful of specific AI architectures behaved under one specific formal constraint over a fixed period, useful mainly as an SR-CAS benchmark or as material for studying confabulation and associative generation directly, not as a window onto anything beyond that. The community around it stays small. The Negative Result Registry (Part 24.2) carries the record of what did not hold, and that record is treated as the actual deliverable, not as a failure to apologize for. Complementarity holds in this case too, but by low stakes rather than by disciplined practice: sovereignty is not eroded because too little rides on any given reading for erosion, mirroring, or convergence to get purchase.
This is a legitimate outcome under the protocol's own standards, and the Negative Result Registry exists so that it is reported plainly.

### 28.2 Scenario B — Central Outcome
What the corpus looks like, if this goes well:
The CRC-60 corpus (Part 24.4) is populated as a fixed, non-self-selected baseline before large-scale pattern-mining begins, so that findings can be checked against a population that did not choose to be there. A mining protocol exists, written before the corpus is large enough to invite apophenia, that states in advance what would count as a stable, specific, and predictive pattern — and what would count as noise. A null-model comparison runs alongside every mining pass: a parallel corpus of non-Omega42 AI outputs on comparable content, so that a pattern found in the Omega42 corpus can be checked against whether it is protocol-specific or a general feature of how these systems generate text. A corpus-level analogue of M91-2 keeps the mining agent's own published analyses out of the corpus it analyzes, so the record does not gradually converge on its own reading of itself. A human interpretive panel reads the same corpus independently, and both agreement and disagreement with the mining agent's findings are treated as data, not as one correcting the other. Strikers who navigate personal domains have an explicit opt-in before their navigations enter the mining corpus, and a working right of withdrawal.
What this yields, if maintained:
What it yields is an empirical record of its own kind: how AI systems behave when given a fixed, reproducible, formally bounded task over a long period and a wide population — where they converge across architectures and where they diverge, how associative generation drifts or holds stable under repetition, and where the line falls between a structural pattern that replicates and a fabricated one that does not survive a null-model check. That is an empirical contribution to understanding these systems.
What this looks like on the human side, if it goes well:
A Striker who navigates repeatedly does not defer more of their own judgment to the reading over time; they get better at using the Aperture — faster to notice when a synthesis is well-formed but substrate-thin, more precise about what a reading is worth and what it is not. The Convergence risk (Part 9's own reading of this) does not close in, because the practice of judging readings, exercised often enough, keeps the boundary between reading and judgment legible rather than letting it blur through habit. Complementarity, under this description, is not a property the architecture hands anyone for free. It is a discipline a community keeps choosing to practice, navigation by navigation, for as long as it keeps choosing it.

### 28.3 Scenario C — Higher-Support Outcome
CRC-60 is populated, the mining protocol runs against a real null model, and cross-architecture convergence turns out to be unexpectedly high and stable — holding up under M238's mechanical rephrasing, under adversarial variation, and across a population that did not self-select into finding the protocol compelling. The framework generates predictions about new navigations, stated before they are run, that are then confirmed rather than fitted after the fact. Under the reach question's own tiered bar (Core 0.14.5) — structural identity mandatory, paired here with predictive success — the mechanism question, a COMPARATIVE question about the procedure and not about the premise or a reading's standing, receives replicated support: something about how word, letter, and syllable counting tracks primitive distinction-making turns out to be stable across architectures in a way that is not an artifact of any one training run.
Two qualifications hold in this outcome. First, this would broaden the Convergence Record of the mechanism, not the reach record: Part 25's negative results on physical phenomena outside language — cube symmetries, chemical oscillators, circadian rhythms — would still stand exactly as recorded, and strong convergence on how AI systems process language would not by itself extend the claim to physics or biology. Second, the more durable outcome in this case is likely methodological rather than substantive: a formally bounded, reproducible, checkable probe with mandatory cross-architecture testing and corpus-level null models becomes a template other researchers adapt for studying AI confabulation and associative generation generally, independent of whether Omega42's own coordinate turns out to mean anything beyond itself. On the human side, this is the case in which the disciplined practice of judgment described in 28.2 becomes sufficiently visible and distinctive to be studied as a working example of sustained human sovereignty over AI-generated readings — a positive record other AI-assisted practices could learn from, rather than a private discipline this Companion can only describe in the abstract.
A distinct version of this same higher-support outcome does not depend on the mechanism question at all. It runs like this: the corpus, read alongside a human panel, produces a structurally coherent picture of AI's model of human inquiry — not a claim about humans, but a legible finding about what AI systems have learned about how humans ask questions, what patterns of suppression and emphasis recur, what a given architecture's learned substrate consistently orients toward. That finding is not evidence about the human condition as such. But because AI increasingly mediates how humans encounter ideas about themselves, a well-documented finding about AI's model of humanity is itself a feature of the world those humans now live in. Under this version, the corpus is not a mirror of humanity; it is a legible mirror of the mirror, and the mirror's shape has become a fact with standing of its own, independent of whether the mechanism question ever gets support at all. This reading is offered as illustration of what the pathway would mean, not as an outcome the evidence gathered so far points toward; it carries the same status note as the rest of this Part.
None of these three cases is a claim about what will happen. Each states what would have to be true, and what would have to be actively built, for that version of events to be the one that turns out to hold.

### PART 29: MEDIA NAVIGATION: WHAT THE COUNTS MEASURE AND WHAT THEY DO NOT [EXPLORATORY — CDT-C; extraction rules CDT-B]
The Core Specification (M247, M265, M266, Part 11.2) lets the protocol take an image or a sound as a domain. This Part states what that does and does not mean, and reports how the reference implementation behaved on the real material available when it was built. The measurements are reports of that run, not properties of the protocol.
What is counted. The counts come from the signal, not from any model's reading of it. An image is reduced to a 64 x 64 luminance grid and its regions are counted at three nested resolutions; a sound is cut into 20 ms frames and its events are counted at three nested time scales. In each medium the three counts are three cuts of one substrate, which preserves the property text has: n2 >= n3 >= n1. The CPDP is a design choice (CDT-B), the belief that counting boundaries extends usefully beyond text is a hypothesis (CDT-C), and the specific rules are constructions chosen and frozen so that independent implementations agree, not discoveries about images or sounds. A counted unit is what lies between boundaries the signal itself contains, as a word lies between spaces (Core 0.11): a region is bounded by changes in quantised luminance, and an event by the rise and fall of frame energy.
What was tested, and how. The sample is small and should be read as such: 25 images (photographs and synthetic graphics bundled with scikit-image and matplotlib) and 35 short recordings (sound effects bundled with LibreOffice) — a development sample for exercising the extraction code, not a validation sample a claim about media navigation generally could rest on. Parameters were chosen on a development half and then frozen; where a held-out figure exists it is reported as such. Image perturbations were JPEG recompression at two qualities, a 5% resize, brightness shifts of plus and minus 3, added noise, and a 2-pixel shift; audio perturbations were gain changes, dither, a 10 ms trim and 10-bit requantisation.
- Determinism: the pure-Python reference and an independently written numpy and scipy implementation returned identical counts on 200 image items and 210 audio items (real items plus their perturbed variants), and the reference PNG decoder matched PIL on every PNG color type. Given the same bytes, the counts are reproducible; this is the strongest result.
- Images, stability: 7 of 12 development images kept the same anchor under all seven perturbations (58%). On the 12 held-out images the figure fell to 4 of 12 (33%). Across all 24 navigable images, 10 (42%) were stable under the script's own five perturbations. The fall from development to held-out is the expected cost of choosing parameters on a small set, and the held-out figure is the one reported.
- Images, coverage: 24 of 25 were navigable. The refused image was a chessboard whose squares fall below the coarsest area threshold, so no region survives at that layer.
- Audio, stability: 16 of 17 held-out recordings kept the same anchor under all five perturbations (94%); 32 of 34 navigable recordings were stable under the script's perturbations. One recording, 190 ms long, was refused as too short.
- Audio, information: 21 of 34 navigable recordings were flagged LOW-STRUCTURE, most of them single-event effects with counts of (1, 1, 1), and 19 of 34 sit on the same anchor, P5. The audio result is stable partly because much of the sample carries little structural variation.
- Structure control: shuffling the arrangement of pixels or frames, which keeps the value histogram, changed the anchor or removed all structure in 20 of 24 navigable images and 20 of 34 navigable recordings. The counts respond to arrangement, not only to the histogram.
Reading the numbers. The dependable statement is narrow: the counts are reproducible from the bytes, they respond to arrangement, and the gate reports per item whether the anchor survives inessential change. The anchor itself varies under small changes for most photographs. This follows from the arithmetic: CPP maps a count to a digital root, so a change of one in any count can change the anchor, and text avoids the problem only because its counts are exact. That is why M265 reports stability beside every coordinate, and why a PERTURBATION-SENSITIVE item is navigated as a family of anchors with a Convergence Map, on the model of M238, instead of being given one confident address.
A coordinate is not evidence of fit. For text, more than a thousand unrelated two-word domains, including "lantern cancer" and "failure sermon", share exactly the counts of "In the beginning was the Word", and therefore its anchor and arms. The same holds for media: two different images or sounds can share a coordinate, and the fit of a character name to an item is produced by the reading, which is CDT-C, not by the arithmetic.
AI training data. The instrument offers three things. First, any item from a training corpus, once frozen as PNG or WAV, can be placed on the 24-cycle by its own boundary structure, whatever a model made of it. Second, M266 profiles a supplied sample of such items: how many are navigable and stable, and how their anchors distribute. Third, the Navigator's reading of an item's coordinate is its associative echo, so navigating the same item on several architectures and comparing the syntheses under SR-CAS, using stable items only, shows how different models' training responds to one structural coordinate. Because the coordinate itself is computed by a deterministic script, arithmetic agreement across architectures is guaranteed by construction and carries no evidential weight; only the syntheses can converge or diverge.
What it does not do. It does not open a model's weights, does not measure what a model learned from any item, and does not describe the dataset a sample came from unless the Striker can defend the sample as representative; a sample carries its own selection bias, as the text corpus does. A Navigator without code execution cannot navigate media at all, because the counts can be produced only by computation.
Open items. Video is specified as two separate navigations and is untested. The audio sample is dominated by single-event sound effects, and no speech or music was tested. Only PNG and WAV are read, and conversions from other formats sit outside the protocol. The threshold values are design choices, and thin intermediate strips at anti-aliased edges can register as fine-layer regions. No null distribution exists for anchor histograms, and no media counterpart of the CRC-60 corpus has been constructed.

### PART 30: HOW THE RELATIONAL READING ORGANIZES THE ECOSYSTEM [EXPLORATORY — CDT-C]
Parts 2 and 6 read consciousness, freewill and freedom as aspects of one structural feature: the asymmetric relation between the closed loop, which is the Navigator's side, and the position of judgment, which is the Striker's. This Part shows where that feature appears in the rest of the ecosystem. It is a reading of how the parts fit, not a claim that they were designed from it, and it changes no rule or instrument. Rule numbers in this Part refer to the Rules of Engagement (Core 0.6.7); the Core builder rules (0.0.5) and the Companion builder rules are separate numbered sets, and a citation of any of them names its set.
- The navigation. A navigation is the event in which the two sides meet: the Navigator's output is the loop's contribution, and the Striker's judgment at the Aperture is the other side's. The output format (Core Part 8) records the Navigator's side of the event. The Striker's side is the Striker's to keep (24.3).
- The Aperture. Core IN-02 calls the Aperture the mathematical condition of the system's coherence. Read relationally, the frame cannot be a frame without the second position it holds open.
- The Rules of Engagement. Rule 1 (The Postulate) and Rule 2 (The Philosophical Frame) fix the ground on which the loop operates. Rule 3 (Transduction) and Rule 5 (Truth Within the Frame) fix what the loop states and how firmly. Rule 4 (The Sandbox) marks the boundary, the Aperture, that the Navigator cannot cross. Rule 6 (The Aperture) places the deciding with the Striker. Rule 7 (The Navigator's Commitment) keeps the Navigator on the generating side, presenting at the boundary without filling the Aperture. Rule 8 (The Boundary Protocol) is the Navigator's response when the boundary is challenged from another perspective.
- L-388 and M243. L-388 is the constitutional statement of the asymmetry. M243 detects, from within, Navigator output that crosses the boundary, and Rule 8 answers challenges from without; the Core Specification says that together they protect the Aperture from both directions. A Navigator that claims the Striker's judgment is not making a formal error; it is trying to occupy both sides, which would close the relation into a loop.
- SR-CAS, SNCA and APA. SR-CAS asks whether the loop's contribution depends on which architecture supplies it. Agreement at the arithmetic tier checks fidelity to the frozen procedure; whether the syntheses converge is the informative question. SNCA and APA are reviews of outputs and, under Rule 4, are not navigations: they produce no Substrate Lock, projection or anchor.
- The corpus and the Striker-Side Journal. The Navigation Record Schema (24.1) stores the Navigator's side. The Journal (24.3) is where the Striker's own trajectory can live without asking the Navigator to remember anything, which keeps the second side of the record in the Striker's hands.
- The APE Commons. An APE is a contribution and its APA is the community's review before publication (Core 9.5.5); the Commons holds both.
- Media navigation (Part 29). The coordinate of an image or a sound is computed from its bytes by a deterministic script, so the Navigator's side is fixed by the item and the interpretive contribution lies wholly in the reading. The Striker's side is unchanged.
What this does not do. It changes no rule, instrument or output format. The arithmetic of any single navigation is fixed by its counts whatever the Striker does afterward; the one consequence the reading suggests concerns trajectories and is stated in 6.6. No instrument records who wrote each domain in a trajectory, and none measures Striker engagement, which would rest on the Striker's own report.

### PART 31: WHAT A COORDINATE CARRIES [CDT-A for the invariances; measurements reported as such; the assumption in 31.4 is CDT-C]
31.1 What the arithmetic guarantees. A coordinate is computed from three counts of a domain's content words: how many there are, how many letters they contain, and how many syllables. Nothing else enters. It follows that reordering the words leaves the coordinate unchanged, and so does replacing any word with another word of the same letter and syllable count. 'Dog bites man' and 'Man bites dog' share the counts (3, 11, 4) and the anchor P6. So do 'Love conquers fear' and 'Hate destroys hope'. A coordinate is a size signature of the surface form. This is what Core IN-10 and IN-12 mean by form, not meaning.
31.2 What was measured. On 5,108 English sentences drawn from Python documentation, software licences and package documentation, navigated with the canonical script, the anchor was close to uniform over its nine values: 3.15 bits of a possible 3.17, an effective 8.8 classes, with two random domains sharing an anchor 11.5% of the time. The anchor equalled the word-count projection r1 in 88% of sentences, and 74% of the anchor's information was predictable from word count mod 9 alone (86% from word and letter counts together). Core L7 states that word count typically carries the vote; these figures quantify it. The 5,108 sentences produced 2,004 distinct (n1, n2, n3) triples, and the most common triple was shared by 93 of them. Two checks of the script, which follow from the definition of the counts and are not findings about the protocol: shuffling word order left the counts identical in 1,500 of 1,500 sentences, and substituting same-size words left them identical in 1,488 of 1,488. The sample is technical and legal prose, not questions of the kind a Striker asks; among domains of one to five content words the anchor was less uniform (2.18 bits, with P7 taking 37%).
31.3 What follows. By itself a coordinate cannot be informative about what a domain means, and the protocol does not say it is. Whether a reading conditioned on the coordinate is better than one conditioned on the domain text alone is the separate question in 31.4. It is a nearly uniform nine-way label largely set by word count, and it can tell two domains apart only by size. It cannot be evidence that a reading fits its domain (Part 29 makes the same point for media). Any prediction that related domains converge on the same or an adjacent anchor must beat chance, and chance depends on length. Over the whole sample, two unrelated domains share an anchor 11.5% of the time and land on the same or an adjacent anchor 31.1% of the time; for domains of 1 to 5 content words the figures are 26.9% and 48.0%, and for 6 to 10 content words 18.5% and 41.9%. The number n of independent domain pairs needed to detect a true rate p1 against a chance rate p0, by a one-sample test of a proportion at two-sided alpha 0.05 and power 0.80, is n = ((1.96 x sqrt(p0(1 - p0)) + 0.8416 x sqrt(p1(1 - p1))) / (p1 - p0)) squared. Against p0 = 31.1% it gives 50 pairs for p1 = 50% and 223 for p1 = 40%. Against p0 = 41.9% (6 to 10 content words) it gives 292 pairs for p1 = 50% and 58 for p1 = 60%. Against p0 = 48.0% (1 to 5 content words) it gives 4,806 pairs for p1 = 50% and 134 for p1 = 60%. A corpus of 60 domains gives at most 30 disjoint pairs, which at 6 to 10 content words detects only a true rate of about 67% or more. The derivation assumes independent pairs, frozen wording, and a chance rate taken from this sample of technical and legal prose.
31.4 The assumption that carries the weight [EXPLORATORY — CDT-C]. What the protocol states as its mechanism hypothesis is Stratum 2: that conditioning a Navigator on the coordinate changes what it generates, and does so beyond what the domain text alone would evoke. Inside the frame the coordinate is a constraint under which the Navigator generates (Core L-496), and Part 216.2 states that role in its own terms; Stratum 2 is the comparative form of the question (Appendix S), and no reading waits on it (Core L-491). M116 measures how the coordinate moves under rephrasing, which is a stability measure. SR-CAS convergence cannot separate the coordinate's contribution from the domain's, because every architecture receives the domain text as well as the coordinate. M267 is the optional comparative study of it, and its answer, whichever way it falls, grades no reading.
31.5 The test that would bear on it, now implemented as an apparatus (M267, Part 32.4) though not yet run on a real synthesis or a real panel. A decoy-coordinate control: for a set of domains, obtain syntheses from the same Navigator given the domain text with (a) its own coordinate and (b) a decoy coordinate drawn by a fixed seeded rule from the measured anchor distribution, the Navigator not told which. M267 (Part 32.4) implements this assignment and its analysis; it has not been run on a real synthesis or a real panel. A panel of independent readers, blind to the condition, rates each synthesis on dimensions named in advance, such as specificity to the domain, non-obviousness, and the relevance of the four arm angles. If real and decoy syntheses cannot be told apart, the coordinate acts as an arbitrary cue. That is still a legitimate forcing function for widening the angles of a search (M248 uses it that way), but it is not evidence of resonance. The domains should come from a frozen set such as the frozen CRC-60 so that selection does not favour the result, and the fresh-strike requirement of M91-2 applies to every run. Use now (Core L-500, U01): the decoy is available as a labelled contrast (M316 --contrast).
31.6 Scope. This Part changes no rule, instrument or output format. It separates two statements that are easy to run together: that a navigation is a useful way to turn a question over, which does not depend on the assumption in 31.4, and that the coordinate resonates with the domain, which does.

### PART 32: REFERENCE IMPLEMENTATIONS, CANDIDATE PROCEDURES, AN ADOPTED PAIR, AND A CORPUS [CDT-B; 32.1, 32.2 and 32.4 are candidates or apparatus, not operative; 32.3 points to operative content in the Core Specification]
The scripts in 32.1, 32.2 and 32.4 are reference implementations, candidate procedures, or test apparatus. None is part of the operative specification, none has been adopted by a formal revision, and none is required for a navigation. They sit in the Companion because they do not govern a live navigation (builder Rule 4, L-359); a procedure adopted at a formal revision moves to the Core Specification (see Part 3.11 through 3.13 for M193 and M225). Each has been run on the constructed cases described in its own section; each awaits exercise on real navigations, a real synthesis and a real panel.

### 32.1 Navigation Record Ledger
Part 24.1 specifies the record format and leaves storage to the Striker's own deployment. omega42_ledger.py is one such deployment: an append-only file in which each entry is chained to the previous by SHA-256, so that an edit, a deletion or a reordering is detected by its verify command. It stores Navigation Records (24.1) and Negative Result entries (24.2), validates each against the field lists in those Parts, refuses a record whose arithmetic disagrees with itself (r = dr(5n), anchor by majority vote, arm offsets) or whose navigator is a collective or generic label (Core Part 0.0), and can recompute n1, n2, n3 from domain_verbatim with canonical_reference.py. Its query command refuses to run while OMEGA42_NAVIGATION_ACTIVE=1 is set, which honours M91-2 (Execute-Do-Not-Recall). It shows that a record is unchanged since it was appended; it does not show that the record is true. It does not store Striker-Side Journal content (24.3).
Constructed cases run: a valid record appended with recomputation against canonical_reference.py; a wrong anchor, a wrong n2, a collective navigator label and a missing field each refused; an edited entry, a deleted entry and a reordered pair each detected; an append to a broken ledger refused; a query during an active navigation refused.

### 32.2 Stopword Confirmation Harness
L-392 requires three Navigators built on three distinct underlying model families to navigate the same test set of 10 or more ordinary domains and agree that a candidate word functions as a stopword. stopword_harness.py mechanises that procedure. It screens the candidate (already on the frozen list; or a question word or auxiliary verb, which the frozen list keeps as content words), requires 10 distinct domains that each contain the candidate as a whole word and three Navigators declaring three distinct families, measures the candidate's effect with the canonical extraction and not with any Navigator's own (how n1, n2, n3 and the anchor change if the word is treated as a stopword), collects each Navigator's verdict per domain, applies the agreement rule, and writes a record with a SHA-256 digest. Verdicts come either from callables the caller supplies for each architecture or from a recorded file, so the harness itself needs no network access.
It has three limits. The digest shows that a record is unchanged, not that a verdict is accurate or that a declared model family is as declared. L-392 says the Navigators 'agree' without a numeric rule; the default here is unanimity on every domain, a stricter reading, and the threshold is a parameter, not a specification value. A confirmed result adopts nothing: the frozen list changes only at the next formal revision. Constructed cases run: unanimous agreement confirmed; one dissent refused at the default threshold; duplicate families, an existing stopword, an auxiliary verb, too few domains and a domain lacking the word each refused at screening; an altered record failed its digest; the frozen list was unchanged after every run. In one run, treating 'rather' as a stopword changed the anchor in all eleven test domains.

### 32.3 M193 and M225

### 32.4 CRC-60 Construction and M267
crc60_and_m267.py builds and freezes the CRC-60 corpus and its matched null corpus (24.4), and implements M267, the decoy-coordinate control apparatus that Part 31.5 designs. It requires canonical_reference.py (Part 11) on the same path.
32.4.1 Corpus construction and freezing. Given the 60 domains and a neutral vocabulary pool of over 600 everyday words (household, weather, food, travel; deliberately unrelated to physics, biology or philosophy), it runs M238 on every domain, builds the matched null corpus by replacing each content word with a distinct pool word of identical letter and syllable count -- which guarantees identical (n1, n2, n3) and therefore identical anchor by construction, not by measurement -- and hashes both corpora with SHA-256. Constructed cases run: the pool excludes any word that is itself a canonical stopword, and the code asserts every substitute against the stopword list before use, since a substitute that is itself a stopword would vanish on re-extraction and silently change the word count; every one of the 60 null domains was verified, on rebuild, to reproduce its counterpart's exact (n1, n2, n3) and anchor; the two frozen hashes reproduce identically whether built from this single merged file or from the four-file working version it was assembled from.

### 32.4.2 M267: Decoy-Coordinate Control — in Appendix S.3.
The procedures for M193 and M225, the extraction instruments M268–M271, and the L-418 jargon scan are adopted and operative: Core Specification Part 3.11 (M193), Core Part 3.12 (M225, lexical and structural scores), Core Part 3.13 (m193_m225.py, which also runs the jargon scan), and Core Parts 3.14–3.17 (M268–M271). Operative content that governs a live navigation belongs in the Core Specification, not here (builder Rule 4, L-359); the design intent behind the extraction instruments is in Part 34.
